On 8 August 1965 the Second Battalion returned to the United States at
San Diego, California. The majority of officers and men were transferred
to new commands. During September a Combined Fire Support Exercise was con-
ducted for military representatives of SEATO and this organization provided
the ground maneuver element. During early November 1965 a reinforced platoon
from "G" Company participated as aggressors for the U.S. Army Operation
TENDERTOUCH. During the middle of November 1965 this organization conducted
a PHIBLEX off the USS PRINCETON. Three rifle companies and elements of H&S
Company participated; however, companies were far below the manning level.
On 15 November 1965 the Regimental Landing Team-5 special training program
was implemented; however, due to personnel TAD to schools, commitments of
higher authority, and on board strength of approximately 50%, training was
very limited.
The Third Battalion, Ninth Marines was redesignated the Second Battalion, Fifth Marines. Lieutenant Colonel C. E. MC PARTLIN, Jr., was the Commanding Officer.

attachments commenced prior to this date. Reference (d),

Training aboard ship was limited to formal instruction and physical training. Formal instruction was accomplished on general military type subjects, Viet Nam orientation, and Landmine Warfare. Training began upon arrival on Okinawa on 2 February 1966, all units are accomplishing field training and field firing. Crew served weapons personnel have completed a one week organizational level school, and the majority of personnel have fired their T/O weapon for battle sights. The first rifle company is undergoing Counterguerrilla Warfare School in the northern training area which is scheduled for all units.
rows.note: Shipboard/Okinawa training occurs after cutoff.

rows.quote: Several items of supplies and individual equipment that were left in WESTPAC by this organization in July 1965 were missing when the Battalion received the warning order. Priorities on requisitions were upgraded by messages since they had been on order since August 1965. Priorities generated by the warning order released many of these items, but this organization was still short some items of 782 gear upon embarkation. The BATTALION LANDING TEAM had 93% of its operating stocks and 98% of its mount out. All shortages were non-essential combat equipment items. They were: Sniperscope Batteries, Suspender Straps, Tent Pins, Bayonet Scabbards, and Mess Pans.
rows.note: Shortages at embarkation are subsequent outcomes; pre-departure requisition activity is included with an approximate interval.

rows.quote: A PU-348 generator previously invoiced to REGIMENTAL LANDING TEAM-1 was replaced with a PU-239. Nineteen new M-416-B-1 trailers were received by this organization. However, due to the fact that no spare parts were available for the new trailers, both the M-416-B-1 and M-100 trailers were embarked. An additional 30 days operating stock was ordered. Eighty percent of these requisitions were filled prior to embarkation.

The following mount-out blocks were ordered, embarked, and in
some cases packed, which were not previously held by this
organization. These were:
    (1). 30 day class I
    (2). 30 day 1st through 3rd echelon class II spares
    (3). 30 day dry cells
    (4). 4 day class III
    (5). 30 day class IV
    (6). 30 day class V
At the time the Battalion received the warning order, the
embarkation Officer was on leave. Several minor difficulties
were encountered during the embarkation planning due to lack of
experience of the embarkation team and the relatively short notice
given. As directed by the warning order, the ships were combat
loaded. This presented numerous embarkation problems, as the
exact cargo load was not known early in the planning stages, and
was changed several times after loading plans were completed.
These changes were due to the fact that supplies back ordered for
this organization were still arriving at Camp Pendleton as late as 7
January 1966. Cargo ordered for other 1st Marine Division units
was ordered loaded on a space available basis, thereby complicating
embarkation procedures.

The BATTALION LANDING TEAM S-4 Officer and S-4 chief were left
behind to secure the camp and upon completion, flew to Okinawa to
make arrangements for our debarkation there. References (e), (f),
and (g) were sailing reports from the USS BEXAR (APA-237, USS
MATHEWS (AKA-96) and USS BELLE GROVE (LSD-2) respectively. These
